newsitem.title: UK: Dlr firms as German asset deal fans weak-euro fear.
newsitem.headline: Dlr firms as German asset deal fans weak-euro fear.

text.p: The dollar zipped higher against the mark in morning Europe as market fears of a wide, weak single currency were fanned by Bonn's apparent failure to use revaluation of central bank assets as help in qualifying for EMU.

Talks between the Bundesbank -- which bitterly opposed the plan -- and the German government produced an agreement that the payout from the revaluation would only be in 1998. Founding members of the euro will be chosen on the basis of 1997 data.
The development makes Germany's task of meeting EMU deficit goals tougher, and increases the risk of a flexible interpretation of entry criteria and a soft euro, analysts said.
"The government's backed down, the Bundesbank has won the round and now the Germans have to go back to the drawing board," said Nick Stamenkovic, economist at DKB International.

With chances looking ever higher that a broad swathe of countries will launch the euro in 1999, the mark remained depressed by the prospect of being subsumed into a weaker unit -- and that was all good news for dollar/mark.
"The underlying tone of the dollar looks good, it's being helped by worries about the euro and should be supported by evidence of strong U.S. growth," said Stamenkovic.
The dollar was quoted at 1.7322/32 marks at 0804 GMT.
That was up from late Tuesday's European level of 1.7274/84, though just off an early peak of 1.7340.
The probe above yesterday's high of 1.7330 marks set the U.S. unit's sights on its 1997 peak of 1.7389, hit on April 28.
But whether it can find the momentum to power through those levels just yet depends to a large extent on the May U.S. non-farm payrolls report, due out Friday, analysts said.

Adrian Schmidt, international economist at Chase, said data such as the May Redbook Retail Sales Index, released Tuesday, had been disappointing and put a dampener on expectations of Federal Reserve tightening.

"I don't think people are that confident the U.S. side is going to be particularly positive, so I'm not sure the dollar will rush through the highs, but we would certainly look for 1.75 marks in a month or so," said Schmidt.

Seasonal adjustments by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics have prompted many economists to lower their payrolls forecasts, but the consensus of expectations gathered by Reuters still points to a hefty 221,000 increase after April's 142,000 rise.
Back in Europe, the market was nervously watching France, where new Socialist Prime Minister Lionel Jospin was likely to name the members of his government.

The left-wing victory in Sunday's French election pumped up fears of a weak euro, as the Socialists have pushed for Spanish and Italian membership of EMU from the outset and set their face against fresh economic austerity measures.
Concerns are now focused on the role the Communists -- who hold the balance of power and are opposed to the single currency -- will play in France's new government.
German Finance Minister Theo Waigel insisted Germany still demanded a strict interpretation of EMU entry criteria, and would meet those goals.
The European focus kept dollar/yen sidelined.

It was quoted at 116.23/33 yen at 0851 GMT compared with late Tuesday's European level of 116.09/19. Analysts said the belief that the Japanese authorities were comfortable with dollar/yen's current levels should keep it rangebound.

Elsewhere, the mark fell on the European crosses but pulled off lows after Waigel said Germany would meet EMU goals strictly. It firmed against the Swiss franc, however, as the market mulled the Swiss National Bank's recent vow to loosen monetary policy if EMU fears led to a renewed flight to francs.
-- Abigail Levene, London Newsroom +44-171-542-8968
